facts.user_claim: So it's just a scaling law.
facts.fact: Scaling laws are real and predictive. In January 2020, Kaplan et al. showed that model error falls smoothly as a power law with model size, data and compute. OpenAI said it predicted parts of GPT-4's performance from models trained with no more than 1/1,000th of GPT-4's compute. Scale is not the whole story, though. Human-feedback fine-tuning, built on real users' prompts and human rankings, turned raw models into useful assistants.

facts.user_claim: NEW: do NOT repeat 'humans now have an 8-second attention span, shorter than a goldfish'
facts.fact: The popular claim that humans have an 8-second attention span, shorter than a goldfish's 9 seconds, has no research behind it. It traces to a 2015 Microsoft Canada consumer-insights report, which credited a website called 'Statistic Brain'. BBC and Wall Street Journal investigations in 2017 found no study supporting the numbers.
facts.evidence_card: MYTH: '8-second human vs 9-second goldfish' · No study behind it · Source: BBC World Service, 'Busting the attention span myth' (10 March 2017)

sources.supporting_quote: Popular accounts claiming the average person's attention span has dwindled to 8 seconds—shorter, supposedly, than a goldfish—are not corroborated by science.

facts.caveats: Changes: I swapped the downes.ca repost for the BBC original URL, because that repost is dated 10 Feb 2023, not 2017. facts.fact: In a 2008 lab study, Gloria Mark and colleagues found that interrupted people finished tasks faster with no difference in quality. But they paid for it with more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort.

facts.caveats: Verified against the paper's text, including 'Forty-eight subjects participated' and the abstract quote, which I corrected to its exact wording. I added that most subjects were German students. This is a small lab experiment using an email task. Do not use the widely quoted '23 minutes to refocus' figure; the UC Newsroom piece says only that recovering from an interruption 'can take almost half an hour'.

facts.fact: In an MIT Media Lab EEG study of 54 people writing essays, brain connectivity was weakest when people used ChatGPT and strongest when they wrote unaided. In the first session, 15 of 18 ChatGPT users (83%) failed to quote from the essay they had written minutes earlier, compared with 2 of 18 in each of the other groups.

sources.supporting_quote: Brain connectivity systematically scaled down with the amount of external support ... In the LLM-assisted group, 83.3 % of participants (15/18) failed to provide a correct quotation, whereas only 11.1 % (2/18) in both the Search-Engine and Brain-Only groups encountered the same difficulty.

sources.supporting_quote: it has not yet been peer-reviewed, thus all the conclusions are to be treated with caution and as preliminary.

facts.caveats: Verified in the v2 PDF. The supporting quotes come from the paper's summary and results sections, not its abstract; the abstract says 'Cognitive activity scaled down in relation to external tool use.' Changes: I reworded the recall finding to match the paper (failing to quote at all) and added the stricter result that none of the 18 gave a fully correct quote. The v2 PDF (Dec 31, 2025) is still marked 'Preprint, under review', and the FAQ says peer review has only begun. I could not run new searches to check for a 2026 journal version. Narrate it as 'early evidence suggests'.

facts.user_claim: Research brief: Microsoft Research and CMU CHI 2025 study found higher confidence in AI goes with less critical thinking
facts.fact: Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon surveyed 319 knowledge workers about 936 real examples of using generative AI at work. The more people trusted the AI, the less critical thinking they reported doing, while people confident in their own skills reported more.
facts.evidence_card: CHI 2025 · 319 knowledge workers: more trust in AI = less critical thinking · Source: Lee et al., Microsoft Research & CMU
key_numbers: Critical thinking self-reported in 555 of 936 examples (59.29%)

sources.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
sources.publisher: ACM CHI 2025 / Microsoft Research (Lee, Sarkar, Tankelevitch, Drosos, Rintel, Banks, Wilson)
sources.supporting_quote: Specifically, higher confidence in GenAI is associated with less critical thinking, while higher self-confidence is associated with more critical thinking.

facts.caveats: Verified on the Microsoft page and in the author PDF (319, 936, 555 = 59.29%, Article 1121, DOI 10.1145/3706598.3713778). I corrected '~60%' to the exact 59.29%. This is a self-reported, correlational survey, so it shows an association, not that AI causes a decline. The authors also find that critical thinking shifts toward verifying and integrating AI output rather than disappearing. Do not use the unverified '83 of 319' or '36%' numbers circulating online.

facts.user_claim: NEW (one-line framing for the 'use it or lose it' idea)
facts.fact: The same Microsoft paper cites a decades-old 'irony of automation': when machines do the routine work, people lose the daily practice that keeps their judgement sharp. That leaves their skills weakened when the hard cases arrive.
facts.evidence_card: '...leaving them atrophied and unprepared when the exceptions do arise' · Source: Lee et al., CHI 2025, on Bainbridge's 'Ironies of Automation' (1983)

sources.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (PDF)
sources.supporting_quote: As Bainbridge [7] noted, a key irony of automation is that by mechanising routine tasks and leaving exception-handling to the human user, you deprive the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgement and strengthen their cognitive musculature, leaving them atrophied and unprepared when the exceptions do arise.

facts.caveats: Verified word for word in the PDF; reference [7] is Lisanne Bainbridge, 1983, 'Ironies of automation'. These words are the Microsoft authors' paraphrase of Bainbridge, not Bainbridge's own sentence, so credit the on-screen quote to Lee et al. (as the card does), not to Bainbridge. This is a theoretical framing, not a measured result.

facts.user_claim: NEW (2025 follow-up on AI and learning; strongest causal evidence in this cluster)
facts.fact: In a randomized field experiment with nearly 1,000 high-school math students, unrestricted GPT-4 access raised practice grades by 48%. When the AI was taken away, those students scored 17% lower than students who never had it. A tutor version with learning safeguards largely avoided that drop.
facts.evidence_card: PNAS, JUNE 2025 · With AI: +48% · AI removed: -17% vs never-users · Source: Bastani et al., 'Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning'
key_numbers: +48% grades with GPT Base during practice

sources.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
sources.publisher: PNAS (Bastani, Bastani, Sungu, Ge, Kabakcı, Mariman)
sources.supporting_quote: when access is subsequently taken away, students actually perform worse than those who never had access (17% reduction in grades for GPT Base)-i.e., unfettered access to GPT-4 can harm educational outcomes. These negative learning effects are largely mitigated by the safeguards in GPT Tutor.

facts.caveats: Verified the abstract through PubMed (PMID 40560616) and the full text through PMC. The study was an RCT at one large high school in Turkey in fall 2023, using GPT-4, in one subject (math). Change: the August 2025 PNAS correction (e2518204122) only fixed an author affiliation, so it does not touch any results. The point is that design and how you use the tool matter, since the guardrailed tutor largely avoided the harm.

facts.user_claim: NEW (real-world deskilling evidence)
facts.fact: At four Polish endoscopy centres, doctors who had started using AI-assisted colonoscopy found precancerous growths less often in the procedures they did without AI. Their detection rate fell from 28.4% in the three months before the AI arrived to 22.4% in the three months after.
facts.evidence_card: LANCET GASTRO & HEPATOLOGY, AUG 2025 · Detection without AI: 28.4% → 22.4% · Source: Budzyń et al.

sources.title: Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to artificial intelligence in colonoscopy: a multicentre, observational study
sources.supporting_quote: The ADR of standard colonoscopy decreased significantly from 28·4% (226 of 795) before to 22·4% (145 of 648) after exposure to AI ... Continuous exposure to AI might reduce the ADR of standard non-AI assisted colonoscopy

facts.caveats: Verified the abstract through PubMed (PMID 40816301). Changes: I removed 'experienced', because the abstract does not describe the doctors' experience level. I also reworded 'within three months' to the actual design: the 3 months before AI compared with the 3 months after. A correction was published in Sept 2025 (PMID 40946709) with no details shown, but the indexed abstract still carries these numbers. This is a retrospective observational study, so it shows an association. Some secondary sources, such as a 2026 scoping review, wrongly call it a randomized trial; do not repeat that. AI-assisted colonoscopy still finds more growths overall. Say 'skills may fade when we lean on the tool', not 'AI makes doctors worse'.

facts.user_claim: Research brief: Chekroud et al. 2018 Lancet Psychiatry found people who exercise had ~1.5 fewer poor-mental-health days per month, ~43% fewer
facts.fact: In survey data from 1.2 million Americans, people who exercised reported about 1.5 fewer days of poor mental health per month than similar people who didn't, about 43% fewer. Sessions of around 45 minutes, three to five times a week, showed the largest benefit.
facts.evidence_card: LANCET PSYCHIATRY, 2018 · 1.2M Americans: exercisers had 1.49 (43%) fewer bad mental-health days/month · Source: Chekroud et al.

facts.caveats: Verified against the PubMed abstract (PMID 30099000); I only added the data source and years. The study is cross-sectional and self-reported, so it shows an association, not causation. The authors also note 'More exercise was not always better.'

facts.user_claim: Research brief: Singh et al. 2023 BJSM umbrella review found physical activity highly beneficial for depression and anxiety
facts.fact: A 2023 umbrella review pooled 97 reviews covering more than 1,000 trials and 128,000 people. It concluded that physical activity is 'highly beneficial' for symptoms of depression, anxiety and distress, with medium-sized effects compared with usual care.
facts.evidence_card: BRITISH J. OF SPORTS MEDICINE, 2023 · 1,039 trials, 128,119 people: exercise 'highly beneficial' for depression & anxiety · Source: Singh et al.
key_numbers: Median effect size: depression -0.43, anxiety -0.42, distress -0.60
77 of 97 reviews rated critically low quality (AMSTAR)

sources.title: Effectiveness of physical activity interventions for improving depression, anxiety and distress: an overview of systematic reviews
sources.publisher: British Journal of Sports Medicine (Singh et al., University of South Australia)
sources.supporting_quote: Physical activity is highly beneficial for improving symptoms of depression, anxiety and distress across a wide range of adult populations, including the general population, people with diagnosed mental health disorders and people with chronic disease.

facts.caveats: Verified against the PubMed abstract (PMID 36796860). Do not use the press-release line that exercise is '1.5 times more effective than counselling or medication'; the comparison was against usual care, not a head-to-head trial. Also note that 77 of the 97 included reviews were rated critically low quality, and that the benefit faded in longer-running interventions.
